explain: a + b is done in int (integer promotion), so the sum is 300. Storing 300 in uint8_t keeps only the low 8 bits: 300 mod 256 = 44. Unsigned narrowing is well defined, but it is a silent bug. Watch for sensor sums and checksums stored in small types.
title: What does this print?

explain: When int meets unsigned int, the int is converted to unsigned. -1 becomes 0xFFFFFFFF, which is bigger than 1. Typical place: comparing a signed return value (like -1 for error) with a size_t length. Enable -Wsign-compare.
title: What does this print?

explain: An array parameter is really a pointer. The [64] is ignored. sizeof(buf) is the size of a pointer: 4 bytes on Cortex-M (8 on your PC). Pass the length as a separate parameter. GCC warns with -Wsizeof-array-argument.
title: On STM32 (32-bit ARM), what is printed?

explain: ~(1<<4) | 1 is 0xFFFFFFEF. ANDing with that only clears bit 4. Setting a bit with AND never works. Correct: reg = (reg & ~(1u << 4)) | (1u << 0); Clear and set are two different operations.
title: Goal: clear bit 4 and set bit 0. What is printed?

explain: Macros replace text. MS_TO_TICKS(5 + 5) becomes 5 + 5 * 4 = 25. Always put parentheses around each parameter and the whole body: #define MS_TO_TICKS(ms) ((ms) * 4). Or use a static inline function.
title: What does this print?

code: uint32_t mask = 1 << 31;
explain: 1 is a signed int. Shifting a 1 into the sign bit of int is undefined behavior in C. It usually 'works', until the optimizer uses it. Write 1u << 31 or UINT32_C(1) << 31. Register header files use the u suffix for this reason.
title: uint32_t mask = 1 << 31;  — what is this in C?

explain: uint32_t needs 4-byte alignment. So: type(1) + 3 padding + value(4) + crc(1) + 3 tail padding = 12. Reordering fields (value, type, crc) gives 8. Never send a struct over UART or SPI with memcpy: padding and endianness differ between devices.
title: sizeof(Packet) on ARM Cortex-M?

explain: wrapping_add wraps to 0. checked_add returns None on overflow. In firmware, choose on purpose: wrapping_* for counters and timers, checked_* for sizes and lengths, saturating_* for sensor values.
title: What does this print?

explain: The compiler sees the constant values and the deny-by-default lint arithmetic_overflow stops the build. With values only known at runtime: debug builds panic, release builds wrap (unless overflow-checks = true). Many firmware profiles turn overflow-checks on in release too.
title: What happens?

explain: let _ = ... does not bind. The value drops at once, so 'c ' prints first. Then println!() prints a newline. At the end of main, locals drop in reverse order: b, then a. Danger in embedded: let _ = cs_guard(); releases a lock or chip-select at once. Use let _guard = ... instead.
title: What does this print?

explain: as never fails. It silently keeps the low bits: 0x0FFF becomes 0xFF = 255. A value of 4096 would give 0! Use u8::try_from(adc) to catch it, or scale on purpose: (adc >> 4) as u8.
title: 12-bit ADC value. What does this print?

explain: data_ready is changed in an ISR, but the compiler does not know that. With -O2 it reads the flag once and the loop becomes while(1). Mark flags shared with an ISR as volatile. Note: volatile prevents caching, but it does NOT make multi-byte access atomic.
title: Works with -O0, hangs with -O2. Tap the bug.

explain: When head == 64 it does not reset, so the next push writes buf[64], one byte past the end. Valid indices are 0..63, so the check must be >=. Tip: with a power-of-2 size, use head = (head + 1) & (BUF_SIZE - 1);
title: Ring buffer. Memory after buf gets corrupted. Tap the bug.

explain: ODR |= is read-modify-write: load, OR, store. If the timer ISR toggles PA5 between the load and the store, main writes back the old PA5 value and the toggle is lost. On STM32 use BSRR. It sets or resets single pins in one atomic write.
fix:
GPIOA->BSRR = (1u << 6);          // set PA6
GPIOA->BSRR = (1u << (6 + 16));   // reset PA6
title: LED on PA5 sometimes stops blinking. Tap the bug.

explain: On an 8-bit MCU, reading a uint32_t takes 4 separate loads. If the ISR fires in the middle (for example 0x000000FF to 0x00000100), you get a mix of old and new bytes. volatile does not help here. Read it with interrupts disabled.
title: AVR (8-bit). millis() sometimes jumps by 256. Tap the bug.

explain: Writing DR only puts the byte in the TX buffer. The shift out happens later. CS goes high before the bits leave, so the sensor drops the frame. Wait for TXE and then for BSY == 0 before releasing CS.
title: Sensor ignores every SPI command. Tap the bug.

explain: The stack depth in xTaskCreate is in words, not bytes. 256 words = 1024 bytes on a 32-bit MCU. The local buffer alone is 2048 bytes, so the stack overwrites other memory. Fix: make the buffer static, or give a bigger stack. Turn on configCHECK_FOR_STACK_OVERFLOW = 2 during development.
fix: static char line[2048];   // not on the task stack
title: FreeRTOS on Cortex-M. Random HardFaults. Tap the bug.

explain: Both calls return HAL_StatusTypeDef (HAL_OK, HAL_ERROR, HAL_TIMEOUT). The code ignores it, so on a NAK it parses whatever is left in data[]. Check every bus call and report the sensor as offline. Also check the CRC byte that the sensor sends.
title: Unplug the sensor: temperature shows old values. Tap the bug.

explain: rx_idx is uint8_t, so it can only count to 255. After 255 it wraps to 0 and overwrites the start of the frame. The check rx_idx < 300 is always true. Pattern: when a size constant changes, check every index and counter type that uses it. Fix: uint16_t rx_idx.

pr.author: junior-dev
pr.body: Long Modbus frames were cut off. Bigger buffer fixes it.
pr.title: Increase UART RX buffer to 300 bytes

explain: HAL_Delay counts SysTick interrupts. If EXTI has the same or higher priority than SysTick, the tick never increases and the MCU hangs forever. Even if it works, it blocks all lower interrupts for 20 ms. Pattern: no delays in an ISR. Debounce with a timestamp (ignore edges for 20 ms) or a timer.

pr.author: fw-intern
pr.body: Button triggered 3–4 times per press. Added a 20 ms debounce.
pr.title: Fix button bounce

explain: Good change. BSRR writes are atomic: the low 16 bits set pins, the high 16 bits reset pins, and other pins do not change. No read-modify-write, no race with ISRs. Not every PR has a bug. Learning to approve correct code fast is also a skill.

pr.author: senior-fw
pr.body: ODR |= / &= races with the timer ISR that also writes port A.
pr.title: Use BSRR for status LED

explain: One I2C NAK (EMI, loose cable, sensor brown-out) now panics. In no_std the panic handler usually halts or resets the whole device. The old code degraded nicely. Pattern: 'X is always there' is not true in the field. Return Result and let the caller decide.

pr.author: rustacean42
pr.body: The match was noisy. unwrap() is cleaner, and the sensor is always there.
pr.title: Simplify temperature read

explain: Good change. critical_section::Mutex<Cell<T>> is the standard safe way to share small state with an ISR. Alternative on Cortex-M3 and newer: AtomicU32::fetch_add. Cortex-M0 has no atomic read-modify-write, so the critical section is the portable choice.

pr.author: senior-fw
pr.body: static mut shared between main and the TIM2 ISR is a data race (UB).
pr.title: Remove static mut tick counter

explain: push_back can call malloc inside an ISR: not reentrant, slow, can fail. The vector also grows without limit until the heap is gone. Fixed-size std::array (or a ring buffer) is the right tool here. Pattern: no heap allocation in ISRs, and in hard real-time code no heap after init.

pr.author: cpp-fan
pr.body: Raw arrays are old style. vector is safer and grows when needed.
pr.title: Modernize ADC buffer with std::vector

explain: I2C lines are open-drain: the pull-up resistor charges the bus capacitance. Rise time ≈ R × C. Long wires mean more C, so you need smaller R (for example 4.7k → 2.2k). Do not go below the sink current limit: 3 mA in standard and fast mode.
title: I2C at 400 kHz, long wires. Rising edges are too slow on the scope. What do you change?

explain: R = (Vcc − Vf) / I = (3.3 − 2.0) / 0.010 = 130 Ω. Next standard value: 150 Ω. Also check the GPIO current limit in the datasheet (often around 8–20 mA per pin, plus a total limit per port).
title: 3.3 V GPIO, red LED Vf = 2.0 V, target 10 mA. Resistor?

explain: Vout = 5 × R2 / (R1 + R2). 18k gives 3.21 V, a safe margin under 3.3 V. (20k gives 3.33 V, too close.) 47k gives 4.12 V and can damage the pin. Also keep the source impedance low enough for the ADC sample time, or add a small cap on the ADC pin.
title: 5 V sensor into a 3.3 V ADC. R1 (top) = 10 kΩ. R2 (bottom) = ?

explain: A CMOS input has very high impedance. With nothing driving it, it picks up noise. Enable the internal pull-up (GPIO_PULLUP) or add an external 10k to VCC. Then released = 1 and pressed = 0.
title: Button to GND on an input pin. With the button released, the pin reads random 0/1. Why?

explain: The cap gives fast current during switching edges. Long traces add inductance and make it useless at high frequency. One 100 nF per VDD/VSS pair, as close as possible, with a short via to the ground plane. Add a bulk cap (for example 4.7–10 µF) near the regulator.
options: As close as possible to each VDD pin, short path to GND
On the bottom side, far from the MCU
title: Where do you place the 100 nF decoupling capacitor?

bullets: C/C++: mark it volatile, so the compiler re-reads it every time.
volatile is NOT atomic. Wider than the bus (u32 on AVR, u64 on Cortex-M) → read it with interrupts off.
Read-modify-write (x++, |=) in main is a race → critical section, atomics, or BSRR-style registers.
Keep the ISR short: set a flag or push to a ring buffer. Do the work in main or a task.
title: Data shared with an ISR: 4 rules

bullets: Shared state: what does an ISR or other task also touch?
Integer widths: does a counter, index or cast lose bits?
Blocking: delays, malloc, printf or mutexes inside an ISR?
Error paths: ignored return values, unwrap(), missing timeouts?
Peripheral timing: does the code wait for the status flags (TXE, BSY, RXNE)?
Memory: stack size, buffer bounds, heap after init?
title: Firmware PR review: scan for these 6

explain: DMA writes to RAM, but the CPU reads through the D-cache. Old cache lines hide the new data. This is a cache coherency bug. Invalidate the buffer before the CPU reads it. Keep the buffer 32-byte aligned and a multiple of 32 bytes, or put it in a non-cacheable MPU region.
fix:
SCB_InvalidateDCache_by_Addr(rx, sizeof rx);
process(rx, sizeof rx);
title: STM32H7, D-cache on. DMA RX data is sometimes old. Tap the bug.

explain: IrqLock{}; makes a temporary object. It is destroyed at the end of that line, so interrupts are on again before buf and head change. The RAII guard must have a name to live until the end of the scope.
title: Ring buffer still gets corrupted by the UART ISR. Tap the bug.

explain: buf lives on the stack. The function returns, but the DMA keeps writing to that address. Now it overwrites other stack data. The borrow checker cannot see a raw address given to hardware. Use a 'static buffer (for example from static_cell). Safe HAL DMA APIs require 'static buffers for this reason.
fix:
static BUF: StaticCell<[u8; 64]> = StaticCell::new();
let buf: &'static mut [u8; 64] = BUF.init([0; 64]);
title: After start_rx() returns, other variables get random bytes. Tap the bug.

explain: SysTick keeps running when the main loop hangs. Now the watchdog is always fed and never catches a stuck loop. The watchdog becomes useless. Kick it only from the code path that proves the system works. For long flash writes, kick between pages or use a longer timeout.

pr.author: junior-fw
pr.body: IWDG resets the board during long flash writes. Kick it from SysTick so it never fires by mistake.
pr.title: Stop false watchdog resets

explain: Good change. Adding baud/2 before the divide rounds to nearest: 139 gives about 0.08% error, 138 gave 0.64%. The constexpr function has typed parameters, no macro surprises, and static_assert checks the math at build time. It still compiles to a constant.

pr.author: senior-fw
pr.body: The macro truncates. 16 MHz / 115200 gives 138, which is 0.64% fast. Round to nearest instead.
pr.title: Round UART BRR and check it at compile time

explain: A blocking I2C transfer takes about 0.5 ms at 100 kHz, longer with clock stretching. All interrupts are off for that time: UART bytes overrun, timers jitter. If the driver uses interrupts, it can hang. The I2C peripheral does the bit timing itself, so an ISR only delays it. Keep critical sections a few instructions long.

pr.author: junior-fw
pr.body: An ISR could run in the middle of the I2C transfer. Wrap it in a critical section.
pr.title: Make sensor read atomic

explain: x is promoted to int before ~. So ~x is ~0x0000000F = 0xFFFFFFF0, which is -16, not 0xF0. This is integer promotion. Cast back to the small type before you compare: (uint8_t)~x == 0xF0. Same rule in C.
title: What does this print?

explain: as from u16 to i32 zero-extends, so a = 65520. as i16 first keeps the same bits as a signed value (-16). Then i16 to i32 sign-extends. Two's-complement sensor data needs the signed cast first. Even better: i16::from_be_bytes on the raw bytes.
title: Temp sensor sends a signed 16-bit value. What does this print?

explain: fc = 1 / (2π × R × C) = 1 / (2π × 1 ms) ≈ 159 Hz. Signals above this are reduced by 20 dB per decade. Sample well above 2 × fc. The 100 nF cap also gives the ADC sample capacitor a fast charge source, so 10 kΩ is fine here.
title: RC low-pass before the ADC: R = 10 kΩ, C = 100 nF. Cutoff frequency?

bullets: The buffer must live for the whole transfer: static memory, never a local on the stack. In Rust: a 'static buffer.
D-cache (Cortex-M7): clean the cache before DMA TX, invalidate it after DMA RX. Align buffer and size to 32 bytes.
Or put DMA buffers in non-cacheable memory (MPU). Check the DMA can reach that RAM: on STM32H7, DMA1/2 cannot reach DTCM.
The CPU must not touch the buffer while DMA owns it. Use half/complete flags and work on the other half.
title: DMA buffers: 4 rules

explain: A 1 ms uint32_t tick wraps after about 49.7 days. If start is 0xFFFFFFF0, start + 100 wraps to 84, and millis() > 84 is true at once. This is a tick wraparound bug. Compare the elapsed time instead: millis() - start > TIMEOUT_MS. Unsigned subtraction gives the right result across the wrap.
title: Works for weeks, then after ~49 days every wait_ready() fails at once. Tap the bug.

explain: auto ch makes a copy of each element. The loop changes the copies, and the array stays the same. Use a reference: for (auto& ch : channels). Watch for this in config tables and driver state arrays. The compiler gives no error.
title: enable_all() runs, but no ADC channel is ever enabled. Tap the bug.

explain: STM32 HAL wants the 7-bit address shifted left by one. It puts the R/W bit in bit 0 itself. With 0x76 the bus sends address 0x3B, so nobody answers. Pass BME280_ADDR << 1. Check what each HAL expects: some take 7-bit, some take 8-bit addresses.
title: STM32 HAL. BME280 at 0x76 never ACKs. The wiring is fine. Tap the bug.

explain: Good change. A 12-bit ADC gives up to 4095. 64 samples sum to 262080, which needs 18 bits. The uint16_t sum wrapped, so a high input showed a low average. uint32_t holds the full sum, and the result after / 64 fits in uint16_t again.

pr.author: senior-fw
pr.body: 64 x 4095 = 262080 does not fit in uint16_t. The average is wrong at high input.
pr.title: Fix ADC average for 64 samples

explain: load and store are each atomic, but the pair is not. If the ISR increments COUNT between them, store(0) wipes that event. Cortex-M0 has no atomic read-modify-write instructions. Use critical_section::with around both steps, or the portable-atomic crate with its critical-section feature.

pr.author: junior-fw
pr.body: AtomicU32::swap does not exist on thumbv6m, so the build fails. Replace it with load + store. The ISR still increments COUNT.
pr.title: Build for Cortex-M0 (thumbv6m)

explain: On Cortex-M with STM32, the write to TIM2->SR goes through the bus and can finish after the ISR returns. The NVIC still sees the request and runs the ISR a second time. Clear the flag at the start. If you must clear it late, read SR back or add __DSB() after the write. A new update after an early clear sets the flag again, so nothing is lost.

pr.author: junior-fw
pr.body: Clear the update flag at the end of the ISR, so a new update during the work is not lost.
pr.title: Clear TIM2 flag after the work

explain: Line 5 compiles. 300 is cut to 44 with at most a warning. Brace init does not allow narrowing. 300 does not fit in uint8_t, so line 6 is a compile error. Use brace init for register values and config constants. The compiler then catches values that do not fit.
title: What happens?

explain: chunks_exact(2) gives [1,2] and [3,4]. 0x0201 + 0x0403 = 513 + 1027 = 1540. The last byte 5 goes to remainder() and is skipped with no error. Check remainder() or the length first, or the odd byte is lost.
title: Sum 16-bit LE words from a packet. What does this print?

explain: A CMOS 74HC input at 5 V needs VIH of about 0.7 × VCC = 3.5 V. A 3.3 V output is below that, so HIGH is not guaranteed. 74HCT has TTL levels (VIH = 2.0 V), so 3.3 V works. Or use a level shifter. A series resistor does not raise the voltage.
options: No: 74HC needs about 3.5 V for HIGH at 5 V. Use 74HCT or a level shifter
No: 3.3 V will damage the 74HC input
Yes, if you add a 10 kΩ series resistor
title: 3.3 V MCU output drives a 74HC chip powered from 5 V. Is the logic HIGH safe?

bullets: Keep timestamps in a fixed unsigned type, like uint32_t. A 1 ms uint32_t tick wraps after about 49.7 days.
Compare elapsed time: now - start >= timeout. Unsigned subtraction is correct across the wrap.
Never compare a deadline: now > start + timeout breaks when start + timeout wraps.
In Rust, use now.wrapping_sub(start). Plain - panics in debug builds when it wraps.
Test it: start the tick counter near the wrap, for example at 0xFFFF0000.
title: Tick counters and timeouts: 4 rules

explain: NDTR counts data items, not bytes. sizeof(adc_buf) is 128, so the DMA writes 128 half-words = 256 bytes. That is 128 bytes past the end of the buffer. Use the element count: sizeof(adc_buf) / sizeof(adc_buf[0]). HAL functions like HAL_ADC_Start_DMA also take a length in items.
title: STM32F4. DMA uses 16-bit items (PSIZE = MSIZE = half-word). Variables after adc_buf get overwritten. Tap the bug.

explain: On STM32F4, EN can stay 1 until the current data item is done. While EN is 1, writes to NDTR are ignored. Without the wait, the new length may be lost, and the stream restarts with the old count. Keep the loop: clear EN, wait until it reads 0, clear the flags, then set NDTR.

pr.author: junior-fw
pr.body: EN is cleared by our write, so waiting for it is not needed. Saves a few cycles in the idle-line ISR.
pr.title: Remove busy loop in UART RX restart

explain: Good change. Volatile writes keep their order only with other volatile accesses. The compiler may move normal writes to buf after start(), so DMA reads old data. compiler_fence(Release) stops that. When the transfer ends, use an Acquire fence before reading. On Cortex-M7 with cache, also clean the cache and use a real fence (DMB).

pr.author: senior-fw
pr.body: Sometimes the DMA sends old bytes. The writes to buf are normal writes, start() is a volatile write.
pr.title: Add fence before DMA start (Cortex-M4)

explain: NDTR counts down, so the DMA write index is LEN - NDTR = 4. The data wrapped: bytes 50..63 and 0..3 are new, 18 bytes. wr - rd wraps to 2^32 - 46. Because 64 divides 2^32, % 64 gives the right 18. This trick works only when LEN is a power of two. Otherwise use (wr + LEN - rd) % LEN.
title: Circular UART DMA, 64-byte buffer. How many new bytes? (What does this print?)

bullets: The length register counts data items, not bytes. For a uint16_t buffer, pass the element count.
To change a running stream: clear EN, wait until EN reads 0, then write the address and length.
Clear all old flags of the stream (transfer complete, half, error) before you set EN again.
Peripheral and memory data sizes must match the register and the buffer type. Check the request mapping table for the right stream and channel.
title: Starting a DMA stream: review checklist

explain: A uint8_t can hold at most 255, so i < 256 is always true. After 255, i wraps to 0 and the loop never ends. Use a counter type that can reach the limit, like unsigned int or size_t. -Wextra (-Wtype-limits) warns about this compare.
title: Boot hangs inside clear_lut(). Tap the bug.

explain: now and start are promoted to int before the subtraction. When the 16-bit counter wraps, now - start is negative, so the check is false. If start is above 60535, the result can never pass 5000, and the loop waits forever. Cast the difference back: (uint16_t)(now - start) > 5000.
title: 32-bit MCU. If the sensor never answers, wait_ack() sometimes never times out. Tap the bug.

explain: [&] captures period_ms by reference. The callback runs later in the ISR, but period_ms lives on the stack of start_blink() and is gone after it returns. The ISR reads whatever is now in that stack slot. Capture by value: [period_ms] or [=].
title: After start_blink() returns, the LED blinks at a random rate. Tap the bug.

explain: Good fix. p[0] is promoted to int, not to an unsigned type. If p[0] is 0x80 or more, p[0] << 24 does not fit in a 32-bit int: undefined behavior. On 16-bit int targets like AVR, << 16 and << 8 break too. Casting each byte to uint32_t first makes every shift safe.

pr.author: senior-fw
pr.body: UBSan reports a signed overflow when the first byte is 0x80 or more.
pr.title: Cast bytes before shifting in rd_be32

explain: C++20 deprecated only some uses of volatile, like ++ or += on a volatile object, and volatile parameters. Reading a volatile register is still fine. Without volatile, the compiler may read *uart_sr once and loop forever. Keep volatile on hardware registers. Fix the warning lines instead.

pr.author: junior-fw
pr.body: C++20 deprecated volatile, so I removed it to fix the warnings.
pr.title: Remove deprecated volatile (C++20)

explain: Not the same. In debug builds overflow checks are on, so now - start panics when the tick counter wraps. Release wraps only because overflow-checks is off by default, and a profile can turn it on. wrapping_sub says the wrap is wanted and works in every build. Keep it.

pr.author: junior-fw
pr.body: Plain minus is easier to read. Release builds wrap anyway.
pr.title: Simplify timeout check

explain: The macro becomes two statements. Only led = 0; is inside the if. errors++ always runs, so the output is 1 1. Wrap multi-statement macros in do { ... } while (0), or use a static inline function.
title: Status is OK. What does this print?

explain: Division rounds toward zero: -7 / 2 is -3. Right shift rounds toward minus infinity: -7 >> 1 is -4. So x >> 1 is not x / 2 for negative x. C++20 defines this shift. In C and older C++, shifting a negative value right is implementation-defined.
title: C++20. Halve a signed control error two ways. What does this print?

explain: Current in a coil cannot stop at once. When the transistor turns off, the coil makes a high voltage spike on the collector, often above the transistor's Vce limit. A flyback diode across the coil gives the current a path and clamps the spike near 12.7 V. Every relay, motor or solenoid needs one.
options: A diode across the coil, cathode to +12 V
A 100 nF capacitor on the base
title: MCU switches a 12 V relay coil with an NPN transistor. The transistor dies after some weeks. What is missing?

bullets: Each pin has a max current, and the whole chip has a total limit. Read both in the datasheet.
An LED needs a series resistor: R = (Vcc - Vf) / I.
Motors, relays and buzzers draw too much current. Drive them with a transistor or MOSFET.
Coils (relay, motor, solenoid) need a flyback diode across them.
For a MOSFET, check that RDS(on) is given at your gate voltage (like 3.3 V), not only Vgs(th).
title: Driving loads from a GPIO: 5 rules

explain: &rx[1] is not 4-byte aligned. Cortex-M0 faults on any unaligned 32-bit load. The cast also breaks strict aliasing rules. Copy the bytes with memcpy into a local uint32_t, or build the value from bytes with shifts.
title: Cortex-M0. get_value() causes a HardFault. Tap the bug.

explain: bus is passed by value, so a copy is made. When log_byte returns, the copy's destructor turns the SPI clock off. Take SpiBus& instead. Also delete the copy constructor and copy assignment, so this mistake does not compile.
fix: void log_byte(SpiBus& bus, uint8_t b)  // + SpiBus(const SpiBus&) = delete;
title: After the first log_byte() call, SPI stops working. Tap the bug.

explain: heapless::Vec has a fixed size. push returns Err(b) when it is full. let _ = throws the error away, so the line is cut with no warning, and handle_line runs a broken command. On Err, set an overflow flag and drop the whole line at the next newline.
title: Commands longer than 32 bytes run with wrong arguments. Tap the bug.

explain: Good change. With 100, head & 99 skips some slots and gives wrong indexes. 128 works with the mask. static_assert stops the build if someone changes the size to a value that is not a power of 2. constexpr also gives the size a real type, unlike #define.

pr.author: fw-lead
pr.body: The index uses a mask, so the size must be a power of 2. 100 was wrong. Add a compile-time check.
pr.title: Make RX size a power of 2 and check it

explain: EGR = UG loads the new prescaler, but it also sets the UIF flag (with URS = 0). Without the SR clear, the update interrupt fires at once after enable, one period too early. Keep the clear between EGR and DIER. Always clear pending flags before you enable an interrupt.

pr.author: junior-fw
pr.body: SR is 0 after reset, so this write does nothing.
pr.title: Remove useless SR clear in timer init

explain: write_read uses a repeated START, with no STOP between the write and the read. Two calls put a STOP in between. Some sensors reset the register pointer on STOP. On a shared bus, another task or master can also take the bus in the gap. Keep write_read.

pr.author: junior-fw
pr.body: Two calls are easier to follow on the logic analyzer.
pr.title: Split register read into write + read

explain: std::accumulate sums in the type of the init value, not the element type. 0ULL gives unsigned long long, so t is correct. 0u gives unsigned int, so u wraps: 6000000000 - 2^32 = 1705032704. Pick the init type on purpose, for example uint64_t{0}.
title: Sum two energy counters. What does this print?

explain: % is the remainder, and it keeps the sign of the left side: -1 % 8 is -1. Used as an index, that is out of range. rem_euclid always gives 0..len, so -1 becomes 7. For wrap-around indexes with negative steps, use rem_euclid.
title: Ring buffer: step one slot back from index 2. What does this print?

explain: A linear regulator drops the extra voltage as heat: P = (Vin - Vout) × I = (12 - 3.3) × 0.1 = 0.87 W. A small SOT-23 package gets far too hot at this level. Use a buck converter, or a lower input voltage.
title: LDO makes 3.3 V from 12 V. Load is 100 mA. How much power does the LDO turn into heat?

bullets: Do not cast uint8_t* to uint32_t*. The address can be unaligned, and the cast breaks strict aliasing.
Cortex-M0/M0+ fault on every unaligned 32-bit access. M3/M4 allow it for LDR/STR, but LDRD and LDM still fault.
Use memcpy into a local variable. The compiler turns it into one load when that is safe.
Or build the value from bytes with shifts. This fixes alignment and byte order at the same time.
Packed structs hide the same problem: a pointer to a packed member can be unaligned.
title: Reading values from a byte buffer: 5 rules
